This page covers the specific U.S. occupation O*NET/SOC 19-2043.00, Hydrologists: researching groundwater and surface-water distribution, circulation, and physical properties, and studying precipitation's form and intensity, infiltration into soil, movement through the earth, and return to oceans and the atmosphere. Official scope: Research the distribution, circulation, and physical properties of underground and surface waters; and study the form and intensity of precipitation and its rate of infiltration into the soil, movement through the earth, and return to the ocean and atmosphere. U.S. wages and employment come from BLS OEWS 2025 and BLS 2024—2034 employment projections presented by O*NET (specific occupation 19-2043.00). Precise mainland Chinese occupational wages were not obtained and are recorded as a visible gap. The jurisdictions and environmental-protection systems are not interchangeable.

To assess your fit for hydrologist work, first complete a verifiable research exercise using public or simulated materials. Set a fictional research question, such as changes in the relationship between groundwater recharge and surface runoff in a watershed and their effects on water supply. Write a step-by-step process from defining the question and hypotheses, designing data collection and monitoring, organizing and analyzing hydrologic data and building models, and interpreting results and uncertainty, through writing a research report with actionable recommendations. Mark each checkpoint and possible problem: insufficient or missing data quality, invalid model assumptions, conclusions beyond data support, field and water-based work safety, and recommendations misread as permits or engineering conclusions. Check whether data quality control, model assumptions and uncertainty, and authorization boundaries for professional conclusions are mandatory; whether environmental, engineering, and legal conclusions beyond your personal or professional scope require consultation or referral; and whether data and analysis form reviewable records. Assess yourself through actual deliverables rather than an interest questionnaire alone.

Fit signals | U.S. O*NET 19-2043.00 tasks and activities center on designing and conducting hydrologic investigations, collecting and analyzing hydrologic data, developing prediction models, preparing research reports and presentations, applying findings to reduce pollution and erosion, and coordinating and supervising professional and technical personnel. Work combines indoor data analysis and outdoor fieldwork. The interest code is IRC (Investigative—Realistic—Conventional); work styles and skills emphasize critical thinking, mathematics, reading comprehension, active learning, and complex problem solving. If you are willing to rigorously analyze data and build models around research questions, handle uncertainty according to scientific standards, and take responsibility for conclusions, these daily demands may align with your working style.

Caution signals | Official scope and tasks involve research conclusions, data and models, and fieldwork. Insufficient data quality or invalid model assumptions, conclusions exceeding data support, recommendations misread as permits or engineering conclusions, or neglect of field and waterside safety may mislead conclusions, cause decision errors, or endanger people. This page therefore addresses data quality, model assumptions and uncertainty, conclusion and authorization boundaries, and field safety separately. The U.S. occupation itself is not marked Bright Outlook. The O*NET summary and employment trends project little or no change (0%) in 2024—2034, about 500 annual openings, and approximately 6,300 employed in 2024. If sustained data analysis, model uncertainty, or outdoor fieldwork would be difficult for you, treat these as real costs requiring careful consideration.

Responsibility assessment | Genuine fit depends on whether you can accomplish three things within the same study: carry out research and data work thoroughly, defining questions and hypotheses, collecting and analyzing data, developing and validating models, and producing reviewable analyses and reports; maintain standards and safety through data quality control, model assumptions and uncertainty, and field and waterside safety under organizational and regulatory requirements; and accept defined professional responsibilities, taking responsibility for your analyses and conclusions while consulting or referring environmental, engineering, and legal conclusions beyond authority. Test this through a verifiable experience, such as completing a step-by-step research procedure and data-analysis log or quality-checking and modeling simulated data, rather than relying solely on an interest questionnaire.

Hydrologists' daily work can be divided into three strands: (1) research and data—designing and conducting hydrologic investigations, collecting and analyzing groundwater and surface-water data, and conducting data quality control; (2) modeling and prediction—developing hydrologic prediction models, measuring and mapping water-level and flow changes, and interpreting results and uncertainty; (3) reporting and application—preparing research reports and presentations, applying findings to reduce effects of pollution, erosion, and sedimentation, and coordinating and supervising technical teams. All three share scientific and quality requirements but produce different outputs: research and data concern evidence, modeling and prediction concern explanation, and reporting and application concern decisions and communication.

O*NET 19-2043.00, Hydrologists: research groundwater and surface-water distribution, circulation, and physical properties; study precipitation's form and intensity, the rate of infiltration into soil, movement through the earth, and return to oceans and the atmosphere. Core tasks include designing and conducting hydrogeologic investigations, studying and documenting water-resource quantities and distribution, developing hydrologic prediction models, preparing research reports and applying findings to reduce pollution and erosion, and coordinating and supervising professional and technical teams. Job Zone Four: considerable preparation needed; SVP range 7.0 to below 8.0.

entries.answer: According to O*NET 19-2043.00, this occupation researches groundwater and surface-water distribution, circulation, and physical properties, and the full precipitation process: form and intensity, infiltration into soil, movement through the earth, and return to oceans and the atmosphere. Typical tasks include designing and conducting scientific hydrogeologic investigations, studying and documenting water-resource quantities and distribution, developing hydrologic prediction models, writing research reports, applying findings to reduce pollution and erosion, and coordinating and supervising professional and technical personnel.

entries.answer: Hydrologic technicians focus on field measurements, sampling, and data organization; water resource specialists produce plans and policy; environmental engineers focus on environmental engineering design and remediation; water/wastewater engineers handle water-supply and drainage engineering and water-treatment systems; environmental restoration planners focus on contaminated-site restoration plans and planning; and conservation scientists focus on ecological conservation. subject.name: Hydrologists
subject.summary: Hydrologists correspond to the specific U.S. occupation O*NET/SOC 19-2043.00, Hydrologists: they research the distribution, circulation, and physical properties of groundwater and surface water, and study precipitation's form and intensity, infiltration into soil, movement through the earth, and return to oceans and the atmosphere. Official scope: Research the distribution, circulation, and physical properties of underground and surface waters; and study the form and intensity of precipitation and its rate of infiltration into the soil, movement through the earth, and return to the ocean and atmosphere. Core tasks include designing and conducting hydrogeologic investigations, studying and documenting water-resource quantities and distribution, developing hydrologic prediction models, writing research reports and applying findings to reduce pollution and erosion, and coordinating and supervising professional and technical personnel. U.S. wages and employment on this page come from BLS OEWS 2025 and BLS 2024—2034 employment projections presented by O*NET (specific occupation 19-2043.00). Precise mainland Chinese occupational wages were not obtained and are recorded as a visible gap; China's qualification and environmental-protection system boundaries are marked separately.
